findings.explanation:
B and D are both documented properties of change set deployment. On B, a change set carries only the metadata types it supports, so parts of an app routinely have to be reconfigured by hand in the target org after the deployment lands.
On D, Salesforce is explicit: "A change set is deployed in a single transaction. If the deployment is unable to complete for any reason, the entire transaction is rolled back." The same sentence has a symmetrical half worth remembering — once a deployment succeeds, all changes are committed and it cannot be rolled back.
A is false in a way that is easy to miss because the product name sounds plausible. Salesforce Connect surfaces data held in an external system as external objects; it moves no metadata and establishes no link between a sandbox and production. What actually connects two orgs for change sets is a deployment connection, which exists automatically between a production org and its sandboxes and must additionally be authorized to receive inbound changes.
C is false as well. Salesforce documents no user-session precondition for a deployment, and change sets are routinely deployed into live production orgs. The only in-flight work it asks you to think about is Apex: a Deployment Settings option controls whether components referenced by pending or in-progress Apex jobs may be deployed.
findings.note:
Key B,D confirmed. This item previously had a defective option set: its original option C read "A deployment connection between source and target orgs must be authorized before change sets can be sent", which Deployment Connections for Change Sets states almost verbatim — giving the question three true options in a "choose 2". Option C has been replaced with a false statement in the same subject area (that all users must be logged out before a deployment), so the item now has exactly two correct answers. Treat the new option C as authored, not original.

Superseded note from the 2026-08-11 pass, kept because its citations still stand: DEFECTIVE ITEM - flagged to the user. Key B,D preserved, but this 'choose 2' has three true options. C is documented almost word for word by Deployment Connections for Change Sets: 'A deployment connection alone doesn't enable change sets to be sent between orgs. Each org must be authorized to send and receive change sets. This added level of security enforces code promotion paths.' Only A is false. The explanation now says so explicitly rather than leaving a learner who picked C thinking they misunderstood the platform. D itself is settled by Deploy a Change Set: 'A change set is deployed in a single transaction. If the deployment is unable to complete for any reason, the entire transaction is rolled back.'

findings.explanation:
Actions added to the Salesforce Mobile and Lightning Experience Actions section of a page layout surface on a record page in specific components, and Salesforce enumerates them.
The Highlights Panel is the main one: "The actions in the highlights panel come from the Salesforce Mobile and Lightning Experience Actions section of the page layout." It renders the page-level action menu - quick actions, productivity actions and standard buttons - in the order the layout lists them.
The Activities component is the second. Salesforce notes that the activity-related actions are deliberately routed there rather than to the highlights panel: "The component can contain Create a Record quick actions that point to the Event and Task objects. It contains Log A Call and Send Email actions." The worked example in Actions in Lightning Experience makes the split explicit - although New Event and New Task are quick actions on the layout, "New Event and New Task don't show up here", in the page-level menu, and instead "The Activities-related actions - Email, New Event, New Task - display on the Activity tab."
Path displays no actions at all. A path is built from picklist steps, up to five key fields per step and up to 1,000 characters of guidance for success; actions are not part of its configuration. A Report Chart is likewise a display component - it renders a chart from a report and hosts no actions from the page layout.
findings.note:
Answer moved A,D to A,C. D is unsupported: Actions in Lightning Experience enumerates every place actions appear on a record page - the highlights panel's page-level action menu, the Activity tab, and the Chatter tab - and Path appears nowhere in it. The Path setup documentation contains no occurrence of the word 'action' at all; a path consists of steps, key fields and guidance text. The deck's explanation asserted that 'The Path component also exposes layout actions associated with each step', which nothing documents. C is documented twice over, in the Standard Lightning Page Components entry for Activities and in the worked example showing New Event and New Task moving off the highlights panel onto the Activity tab. Flagging one soft edge for the user: B is partly true as well, since the Chatter tab carries the standard Chatter actions from the same page-layout section, so this item has three options with some claim and one with none. A,C is the pair the documentation supports for the quick actions an app builder would be adding.

Follow-up on the same day: option B originally read "Chatter", which was a soft edge rather than a clean distractor - the Chatter tab does carry the standard Chatter actions (Post, Poll, Question, Announcement) from the same page-layout section, so a reader could defend it. B has been replaced with "Report Chart", a display component that hosts no actions, leaving exactly two correct options. Treat the new option B as authored, not original.

findings.explanation:
Deletion cannot be gated by an approval process on its own. A classic approval process supports exactly four automated actions - Task, Email Alert, Field Update, Outbound Message - so it can route the decision and record the outcome, but it can neither delete the opportunity nor stop a rep deleting it while the request is pending.
That makes this a two-part build, and only one option can express both parts. A record-triggered flow submits the opportunity for approval automatically, so the rep does not have to remember to; a second record-triggered flow configured to run before the record is deleted then blocks the deletion with a Custom Error element until the approval has come back. Salesforce documents that element for exactly this: "when a user deletes a record that triggers a flow, the flow can return an error message that tells the user why the deletion was not allowed."
Option A fails on a hard limitation rather than on style. Process Builder Record Change trigger offers only two settings - "only when a record is created" and "when a record is created or edited" - and its other trigger types are platform events and invocation by another process. A process cannot run on a delete at all, so it can raise the approval request but can never enforce the gate. Salesforce also ended support for Process Builder on 31 December 2025 and directs new automation to Flow Builder.
Option C pairs the approval with a time-dependent workflow action, which schedules something for later rather than blocking anything, and rests on Workflow Rules, retired on the same date. Option D adds a second approver to a problem whose difficulty was never the number of approvers.
findings.note: Answer moved A to B. The earlier pass kept A on the reasoning that a process genuinely can submit for approval and that the exam key should stand; further checking shows the item is decided by a capability limit, not by tool preference. Process Builder Record Change trigger offers only "only when a record is created" and "when a record is created or edited", and its remaining trigger types are Event and Invocable - so a process cannot run on a delete under any configuration, and option A cannot enforce a gate on deletion however it is built. A record-triggered flow can: it runs on delete and blocks one with a Custom Error element, which uses the same functionality as the addError() method in Apex. The approval process itself deletes nothing either way - Add Automated Actions to a Classic Approval Process lists four action types (Task, Email Alert, Field Update, Outbound Message) and none is a delete. That also disposes of the duplication that made this item ambiguous: A and B are no longer the same design in two tools, because only one of the two tools can reach a delete.
